research_record.score_observations: Inspected the exact Lenard/Dorn saxophone-and-piano first-page image. It says transcribed and edited by Marty Lenard and opens Adagio molto sostenuto in 4/4. The saxophone line has no key signature in this sample. The first twelve bars emphasize held half notes, ties and slurred stepwise movement, with a grace-note figure and a descending/returning eighth-note run in bar 8. Dynamics include mf, f, pp and hairpins. The keyboard initially sustains chords before moving through inner chromatic tones. Inference from the sample: phrase continuity, sustained tone and soft dynamics matter more than continuous fast passagework in this opening. This does not establish the complete arrangement’s range or demands. The public source score, printed pp. 32–33, was also inspected. It supplies violin and cello alternatives with piano or organ, sustained writing, later chromatic grace figures and ornament signs. It is not the saxophone edition. The saxophone sample labels its stave only Saxophone. The public image does not identify which B-flat/E-flat part is shown, so sounding transposition and edition-specific range remain unverified.

research_record.findings: Gregory E. Miller’s 2008 University of North Texas dissertation gives approximately 13 minutes and a Thomas Liley commission. Miller identifies one movement, organized in sections mainly by tempo, and standard rhythmic notation. His appendix maps an introduction, five main sections, and coda across 288 measures. The dissertation documents fingertip glissandos, palms on strings and muted keys in the piano, alongside timbral trill, growling, pitch bending and slap tonguing in the saxophone. Miller reports no recording in 2008. That historical statement does not establish current recording absence. Indiana University’s composer page independently lists the work under 1998; Groth’s opened exact edition gives alto saxophone, piano, Dorn and DORN1398.
research_record.score_observations: Visually inspected dissertation printed pp. 67–69. Its range diagram gives written B-flat3 to C-sharp7, including substantial altissimo. This is an analyst’s diagram rather than an inspection of the complete score. Examples 55–58 explicitly label the saxophone part in written pitch. Example 55 shows a timbral trill on a tied tone, glissando and diminuendo to ppp; example 56 combines chromatic quick notes with a growled sustained ending. Example 57 at m. 145 shows a downward pitch bend with a diminuendo from mf to p. Example 58 at m. 249 shows a descending chromatic run followed by a slap attack at sfz. Only permission-cleared excerpts and the range diagram were inspected; the full 288-measure saxophone part and piano coordination were unavailable.

research_record.findings: The official composer work page states Date written: 26 February 1976 and describes alto saxophone/wind band, also arranged for alto/piano. The seven movements are Scalic Prelude, Folk Song, Moto Perpetuo, Interlude, Gavotte, Dirge and Quick March. Emerson’s exact E66 catalogue confirms alto saxophone/piano and ISMN M570400690. Its D skill label is the retailer’s own approximate ABRSM Grades 6–7 category and is not a SaxoBrain level. A competing historical account by Philip Scowcroft says the piano work was written for a World Saxophone Congress premiere by Paul Harvey and later scored for strings. This conflicts with the official work page’s version history. Use the official composer page for metadata and retain this discrepancy for further primary-score/premiere research.
research_record.score_observations: Public Emerson E66 pages 2 and 3 display single-staff treble-clef saxophone notation, with the product identifying the alto/piano edition. Written pitches are transposed alto-part pitches. Only these excerpts were viewed. Folk Song begins Moderato con moto, quarter note = 108, in common time. The preview shows p cantabile, lyrical slurs, dynamic hairpins, trills, triplets, short ornamental figures and a six-bar rest. Teaching focus inferred from this excerpt: sustained melodic direction and clear transition between plain and ornamented lines. Moto Perpetuo begins Allegro molto, quasi presto, quarter note approximately 114–120, in 3/4. After a three-bar rest, flowing sixteenths run under long slurs, with accidentals, register shifts and f to ff contrasts. Teaching focus inferred from this excerpt: even legato fingers, pulse stability and controlled breaths through long rapid phrases. The excerpts do not show piano notation or all seven movements. Complete written range, ensemble difficulty and presence or absence of extended techniques are unknown.
